newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia braces for another wet season.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia braces for another wet season.

text.p: Indonesian authorities' efforts to prevent a recurrence of floods earlier this year in Jakarta appeared somewhat ineffective when the season's first heavy showers lashed the city last week, residents said at the weekend.
The official Antara news agency said on Friday the heavy rains in the capital raised the possibility of more floods like those in January and February that left up to 30 people dead.

Paulus Aguswinarso of the Indonesian Meteorological and Geophysical Agency said exceptionally high rainfall of 108 mm (4.3 inches) had been recorded over two hours in the city centre on Tuesday. There were heavy showers again on Wednesday and Thursday.
The rain caused immediate flooding of arterial roads, slowing the city's chaotic rush-hour traffic to a virtual standstill.
Long after dusk on Tuesday, long lines of vehicles were crawling from the city centre to the southern residential suburbs. Many commuters said they reached their homes hours after dinner-time.
Conditions were difficult after the showers on subsequent days, but not as bad, residents said.
But it provided an ugly reminder of floods earlier this year during which large areas of the city of 10 million people were submerged under up to two metres (six feet) of water.
The wet season usually begins in early November and peaks in January. Meteorologists said last week's showers signalled the wet season had begun, albeit a few weeks early.
Budi Lim, a Jakarta-based urban designer, said government measures to clean the city's rivers should prevent flooding on the same scale, without actually stopping floods altogether.
"They (the authorities) have taken serious measures to clean out the rivers...we should be able to contain the floods," Budi said. "I hope the government has taken a lesson from early this year."

In preparation for this year's wet season, the government pledged 12 billion rupiah ($5.2 million) for flood control projects aimed at dredging, enlarging and cleaning the capital's 13 rivers and moving illegal squatters from the banks.
But Kompas newspaper quoted Jakarta governor Surjadi Surdirdja as saying that authorities were not in a strong position to deal with the elements because of funding constraints.
"We need a budget five times what we have at the moment to build Jakarta. Flooding is only one of many problems we have," Surjadi was quoted as saying. He did not elaborate.
In the long-term, flooding would continue as long as the city allowed property developers to build in the mountainous areas of West Java to the south of Jakarta, Budi said.
The construction, he said, had led to the destruction of the natural water catchment area, forcing rain waters into the already bulging rivers which flow into Jakarta.

"They (the authorities) have to control the development on the outskirts of Jakarta...the water which should flow into the earth is now flowing into the rivers...it could be two or three times the normal amount," Budi said.
